title: A container packages an application, not an entire machine

sections.heading: Package dependencies
sections.text: An image bundles application code and required user-space dependencies. A running container is an instance of that image; keep durable state outside its replaceable writable layer.

sections.heading: Match the runtime
sections.text: CPU architecture, operating-system family and kernel compatibility still matter. A Linux image does not run natively on every Windows host simply because it is a container.

sections.heading: Control resources
sections.text: Set suitable CPU and memory reservations or limits. Shared-kernel efficiency can improve density, but startup time and isolation depend on the workload and runtime.

remember: Portability requires compatible platforms and externalized state.

title: Choose orchestration separately from container compute

sections.heading: Select an API
sections.text: ECS uses AWS-native task and service concepts. EKS exposes managed Kubernetes APIs and its ecosystem. Existing Kubernetes practices can favor EKS, with operational trade-offs.

sections.heading: Select compute
sections.text: EC2 gives instance-level control and capacity responsibility. Fargate runs supported ECS tasks or EKS Pods without customer-managed worker instances.

sections.heading: Keep ownership clear
sections.text: Serverless compute does not remove image maintenance, permissions, networking, application health or cost control. Match platform constraints before migrating.

remember: Orchestration and compute are two design decisions.

title: ECS turns task definitions into running work

sections.heading: Define the workload
sections.text: A versioned task definition describes one or more containers, their image, resources, ports and runtime settings. A task is a running instantiation of that definition.

sections.heading: Maintain a service
sections.text: A service maintains desired task count and replaces failed tasks according to its configuration. A standalone task can run finite work without a continuously maintained service.

sections.heading: Group the capacity
sections.text: A cluster is a logical grouping for tasks, services and capacity. It is not restricted to a collection of EC2 machines; eligible Fargate workloads also belong to clusters.

remember: Definition describes; task runs; service maintains.

title: A task definition makes deployment requirements explicit

sections.heading: Pin a reproducible image
sections.text: Choose the image reference and compatible platform. A digest identifies immutable content more precisely than a movable tag; ensure the application listens on the declared container port.

sections.heading: Budget the task
sections.text: Specify supported task CPU and memory combinations, container resource settings and essential containers. Add log configuration, environment references and required storage deliberately.

sections.heading: Version and replace
sections.text: Register a new revision for changed settings, then update the service or run a new task. An old running task does not automatically become the new definition.

title: ECS application permissions differ from startup permissions

sections.heading: Use a task role
sections.text: Application SDK calls use the task IAM role, such as permission for one S3 prefix or DynamoDB table. Avoid static keys inside the image.

sections.heading: Use an execution role
sections.text: The ECS or Fargate agent uses the execution role for supported image pulls, log delivery and secret retrieval. Grant startup permissions separately from application data access.

sections.heading: Protect host credentials
sections.text: EC2 container instances have their own instance profile. Restrict metadata access and host privileges; shared-host containers do not become a hard tenant boundary merely because roles differ.

remember: Task role, execution role and host role have different callers.

title: Load-balancer targets must match the task network mode

sections.heading: Map bridge ports
sections.text: On eligible EC2 bridge-mode tasks, a dynamic host port lets multiple copies of one container port share a host. ECS registers the instance and selected host port with the target group.

sections.heading: Target task addresses
sections.text: For awsvpc tasks, including Fargate, use IP target groups for the task ENI addresses. ALB HTTP routing and NLB connection behavior serve different ingress needs.

sections.heading: Validate availability
sections.text: Allow the correct load-balancer-to-target security path and health-check port. Multiple tasks on one host do not protect against that host failing; spread tasks across failure domains.

remember: Bridge targets host ports; awsvpc targets task IPs.

title: ECS network modes change address and isolation boundaries

sections.heading: Compare Linux EC2 modes
sections.text: Bridge uses a container network with host port mappings. Host shares the instance network and its port constraints. None provides no external connectivity or port mappings.

sections.heading: Use awsvpc deliberately
sections.text: Each task receives an ENI and private address, with task-level security groups and Flow Logs visibility. Fargate requires this mode rather than merely defaulting to it.

sections.heading: Check platform limits
sections.text: Windows and external-instance mode support differs from Linux EC2. Account for subnet addresses, ENI capacity and security controls before assuming another task can start.

remember: Network mode changes both connectivity and capacity constraints.

title: A private Fargate task still needs startup connectivity

sections.heading: Reach required services
sections.text: A task must retrieve its image, obtain required secrets and send configured logs. Private placement alone does not create these service paths.

sections.heading: Choose the egress path
sections.text: Use suitable NAT connectivity or supported VPC endpoints. Private ECR pulls commonly need ECR API and registry endpoints plus S3 access for image layers; logs and secrets need their own paths.

sections.heading: Separate network from IAM
sections.text: Check subnet routes, endpoint policies, security-group rules and execution-role permissions. An image-pull error can be a network or authorization problem.

remember: Serverless tasks still need addresses, routes and service permissions.

title: Inject secrets without freezing credentials into images

sections.heading: Reference protected values
sections.text: Use supported Secrets Manager or Parameter Store references in task configuration. The execution role needs retrieval permission and applicable KMS access.

sections.heading: Understand refresh timing
sections.text: Environment-variable injection occurs when a task starts. Rotating the stored secret does not rewrite an existing process environment; deploy replacement tasks or use an application retrieval strategy.

sections.heading: Limit exposure
sections.text: Avoid printing values in logs or embedding them in image layers. Secure diagnostic access and define how a failed rotation or rollout recovers.

title: Choose a service for continuous work and tasks for finite work

sections.heading: Serve microservices
sections.text: An ECS service can maintain replicas behind supported ALB or NLB integrations, with service discovery and configured scaling. Externalize shared state so tasks remain replaceable.

sections.heading: Schedule finite jobs
sections.text: Run standalone tasks for batch-style work or invoke tasks through a supported scheduler. Define retries, idempotency and completion evidence; a schedule does not prove success.

sections.heading: Migrate deliberately
sections.text: Containerize a legacy application, validate dependencies and storage, then test on compatible compute. On-Demand, Spot and eligible commitment discounts describe capacity or billing, not a special Reserved launch type.

remember: Choose the lifecycle before the purchase option.

title: ECS service scaling changes tasks, not the EC2 fleet

sections.heading: Track useful demand
sections.text: Application Auto Scaling adjusts desired task count within configured bounds. CPU, memory or a suitable request/backlog metric should reflect the bottleneck.

sections.heading: Choose a policy
sections.text: Target tracking follows a metric target; step scaling reacts to alarm thresholds; scheduled scaling anticipates predictable time windows. Include cooldowns and startup delay in the design.

sections.heading: Keep capacity separate
sections.text: More desired tasks need available compute and network capacity. For EC2-backed clusters, host scaling is a separate control; for Fargate, quotas and placement constraints still apply.

title: Capacity providers connect task demand to available compute

sections.heading: Manage EC2 slots
sections.text: An Auto Scaling group capacity provider can manage cluster capacity for eligible EC2 workloads. Task placement still depends on resources, architecture and placement constraints.

sections.heading: Protect running work
sections.text: Coordinate instance draining and termination protection where supported. Removing a host before tasks move can interrupt requests or jobs.

sections.heading: Distinguish newer options
sections.text: Current ECS also offers Managed Instances capacity providers. Compare supported features and infrastructure ownership instead of treating every non-Fargate option as manually operated EC2.

remember: Place tasks and scale capacity as coordinated controls.

title: Spot savings require an interruption-tolerant task design

sections.heading: Keep a baseline
sections.text: A capacity-provider strategy can place a base number of tasks on FARGATE, then distribute additional tasks using configured weights including FARGATE_SPOT.

sections.heading: Plan interruption
sections.text: EC2 Spot or Fargate Spot capacity can be reclaimed. Handle termination signals, checkpoint finite work and keep enough healthy replicas across suitable failure domains.

sections.heading: Do not promise fallback
sections.text: Unavailable Spot capacity does not imply automatic replacement by On-Demand capacity. Test the selected strategy, capacity availability and graceful shutdown.

remember: A lower capacity price is not an availability guarantee.

title: ECR access combines identity, repository policy and network reachability

sections.heading: Store and reference images
sections.text: ECR provides private repositories and a public registry offering. An image digest identifies content; tags are references used by build and deployment processes.

sections.heading: Authorize the caller
sections.text: Grant the correct pull or push actions to the actual principal. Cross-account private access requires appropriate identity and repository policies; registry authentication alone does not authorize every repository.

sections.heading: Trace the pull path
sections.text: The runtime must reach the registry and required image-layer storage. Use the ECS execution role for supported agent pulls rather than expanding the application task role unnecessarily.

remember: Authenticate, authorize and connect are separate checks.

title: Image retention must preserve deployable rollback versions

sections.heading: Make versions reproducible
sections.text: Use a versioned release process and suitable tag-immutability settings. Record the deployed digest so an overwritten tag cannot silently change the intended release.

sections.heading: Preview cleanup
sections.text: Lifecycle rules select image sets for supported retention actions. Preview matching images and account for multi-architecture manifests or reference artifacts before activating deletion.

sections.heading: Retain recovery evidence
sections.text: Keep the known-good digest and images needed by running or rollback deployments. A registry cleanup policy does not verify that an application can still redeploy.

remember: An image that cannot be pulled cannot be your rollback.

title: ECR replication distributes images, not the entire application

sections.heading: Configure destinations
sections.text: Private-registry rules can replicate matching images across Regions and accounts. Cross-account destinations need the required registry permissions.

sections.heading: Validate the replica
sections.text: Replication applies to images pushed or restored after configuration; do not assume an existing repository is automatically backfilled. Verify destination image digest before deployment.

sections.heading: Recreate controls
sections.text: Repository permissions, lifecycle rules and other settings need destination configuration or supported creation templates. Deletions and application deployments are separate operations.

title: Scanning findings need a remediation and deployment decision

sections.heading: Choose coverage
sections.text: Basic ECR scanning checks supported operating-system vulnerabilities. Enhanced scanning integrates Amazon Inspector for supported OS and language-package findings and configured rescan behavior.

sections.heading: Inspect current findings
sections.text: Configure registry filters and scan frequency. Use supported finding APIs or console views; a scan event or an old summary field is not proof that an image is safe.

sections.heading: Close the loop
sections.text: Route supported events for triage, rebuild a patched image and verify the replacement digest. Scanning does not patch the image or automatically stop every deployment.

title: EKS manages Kubernetes control-plane availability

sections.heading: Keep the API contract
sections.text: EKS supplies a managed Kubernetes control plane. Kubernetes knowledge helps portability, but IAM, VPC networking, storage and load-balancer integrations remain platform-specific.

sections.heading: Own the workloads
sections.text: You still configure worker compute or Fargate, namespaces, deployments, services, permissions and application health. Managed control plane does not make every Pod highly available.

sections.heading: Design regional recovery
sections.text: An EKS cluster is regional. Use separate regional clusters for multi-Region designs, with image, configuration, state and traffic-routing recovery plans.

remember: A managed control plane does not replace workload architecture.

title: EKS compute choices carry different operational responsibilities

sections.heading: Compare EC2 ownership
sections.text: Managed node groups automate supported node provisioning and lifecycle integration with an Auto Scaling group. Self-managed nodes leave more bootstrap, patching and upgrade work to you.

sections.heading: Use eligible capacity
sections.text: EC2 node groups can use supported On-Demand or Spot configurations. Current EKS Auto Mode manages additional compute and platform functions with its own constraints.

sections.heading: Respect Fargate limits
sections.text: Fargate runs matching Pods without customer-managed worker nodes, but does not support every DaemonSet, storage or privileged-workload pattern. EKS Fargate does not offer Fargate Spot.

remember: A compute option is a feature and ownership contract.

title: Public ingress and private worker placement are separate choices

sections.heading: Expose only intended entry
sections.text: An internet-facing load balancer uses suitable public subnets while application Pods or nodes can remain private. An internal load balancer serves a private access pattern.

sections.heading: Provide required paths
sections.text: Private workers need supported access to the Kubernetes API, image registry, logs and dependent services through appropriate private endpoints or egress.

sections.heading: Protect each hop
sections.text: Validate controller permissions, subnet selection, target type, security groups and health checks. A load balancer in front of unhealthy Pods does not create availability.

remember: Trace client ingress and worker egress independently.

title: Kubernetes authorization and AWS workload identity solve different gates

sections.heading: Authorize cluster actions
sections.text: EKS access configuration and Kubernetes RBAC govern who can inspect or change cluster objects. Scope roles and service accounts to the intended namespace and operations.

sections.heading: Authorize AWS API calls
sections.text: Use supported EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts to grant application permissions. Node IAM permissions are not a substitute for per-workload least privilege.

sections.heading: Match compute support
sections.text: Pod Identity requires supported compute and its agent; it is not supported on EKS Fargate. Restrict node metadata and use an eligible identity mechanism for the selected platform.

remember: RBAC controls Kubernetes; workload IAM controls AWS APIs.

title: Persistent Kubernetes storage needs a compatible provisioner

sections.heading: Declare desired storage
sections.text: A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage. A StorageClass can describe dynamic provisioning through the selected CSI driver; static provisioning is another supported pattern.

sections.heading: Respect EBS placement
sections.text: EBS is AZ-scoped block storage. Schedule compatible Pods with the volume topology and supported access mode; an EBS volume does not become a shared multi-AZ filesystem.

sections.heading: Use EFS appropriately
sections.text: EFS provides supported shared filesystem access, including eligible EKS Fargate Pods. Fargate storage support differs from EC2; EBS-backed Pod volumes are not supported there.

title: Scale Pods and nodes as two coordinated feedback loops

sections.heading: Scale application replicas
sections.text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling uses configured resource or custom metrics. Requests, limits, readiness and startup time influence whether extra replicas help.

sections.heading: Scale schedulable capacity
sections.text: Eligible node autoscaling mechanisms add or replace nodes when capacity is needed. Pod placement constraints, topology and quotas can still leave work Pending.

sections.heading: Protect availability
sections.text: Use suitable replica spreading, disruption budgets and graceful termination. More Pods on one failing node are not equivalent to replicas across failure domains.

title: Container observability connects symptoms to the failing layer

sections.heading: Collect separate signals
sections.text: Application logs, service events, control-plane evidence and container or node metrics answer different questions. Configure supported CloudWatch Container Insights or other collectors explicitly.

sections.heading: Trace a failed request
sections.text: Correlate load-balancer health, service discovery, task or Pod readiness, throttling and downstream errors. A running process can still fail its real request path.

sections.heading: Verify recovery
sections.text: After a change, compare latency, error rate and resource pressure over the relevant period. Preserve logs and deployment identity so a temporary improvement is not mistaken for a fix.

title: App Runner concepts remain useful, but new-customer availability changed

sections.heading: Understand the managed path
sections.text: For existing eligible customers, App Runner accepts supported source code or container images and manages build or deployment, HTTPS ingress, health checks and configured scaling.

sections.heading: Apply the current boundary
sections.text: App Runner closed to new customers from 31 March 2026. Existing customers can continue using it, but AWS does not plan new features; do not teach it as an unrestricted new deployment choice.

sections.heading: Evaluate the migration option
sections.text: AWS recommends evaluating ECS Express Mode. It provisions an application stack using Fargate, an ALB, scaling and networking in your account; validate IAM roles and the resources you will own and pay for.

sections.heading: Configure ingress separately
sections.text: A public service URL and a private incoming endpoint are separate settings. Private ingress uses the supported VPC endpoint and ingress-connection configuration; an outbound connector does not make ingress private.

sections.text: Run an authorized same-tenant request and a cross-tenant negative test. Check application authorization, workload IAM and supported network-policy logs or evidence independently.

sections.heading: Record the boundary
sections.text: Confirm the denied request cannot read another tenant’s records. Preserve policy versions and results, then remove test resources; one network timeout alone does not prove data isolation.

remember: A boundary is demonstrated by both allowed and denied behavior.
